title: Happiness and the future
note: Harari closes Sapiens by asking whether history has made people happier and by speculating that humans may soon redesign life itself. His biochemical view of happiness and his forecasts are his claims, not settled science. Reviewers including Galen Strawson, Christopher Hallpike and Charles Mann criticized parts of the book.

read.title: Happier, or just richer?
text: In the later chapters of Sapiens, Harari asks a question that history books usually skip: did all this progress make people happier? He doubts it. In his view, happiness depends largely on body chemistry and on expectations, so people who gain wealth soon expect more and feel little better. He also points to a Buddhist idea that suffering comes from craving pleasant sensations. These are Harari's claims.

Economists have studied a related puzzle called the Easterlin paradox. Richard Easterlin reported in 1974 that richer people tend to be happier, yet rising incomes across a country do not seem to raise happiness over time. The time-trend part is contested: Betsey Stevenson and Justin Wolfers argue that growth and happiness do rise together. Galen Strawson, reviewing the book, complained that Harari ignores happiness research.

The final chapter looks ahead. Harari speculates that humans may soon replace natural selection with deliberate design through bioengineering, cyborgs and non-organic life, ending Homo sapiens as we know it. He means intelligent design by humans, not creationism. Critics have been sharper elsewhere: anthropologist Christopher Hallpike called the book infotainment, Charles Mann called many assertions unsourced, and Darshana Narayanan reported substantial scientific errors. Even admirers treat Sapiens best as a provocative argument to test against specialists.

q.q: What does the Easterlin paradox say?
o: Richer people are happier, but national growth may not raise happiness

q.q: In the reading, what does intelligent design mean for Harari?
o: Deliberate redesign of life by humans
